e-36.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Even Power
e-36.worked_solution:
The graph $y=x^{12}$ looks similar to an upward parabola, so

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \infty} x^{12} = \infty .
$$

However, multiplying by the negative coefficient $-12$ causes $y=-12x^{12}$ to look more like a downward parabola. This changes the sign of the limit. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(-12{x}^{12})=-{lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{12})=-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

e-37.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Odd Power
e-37.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{3}}{2} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2}\cdot {x}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y=x^3$ is power function with an odd positive power and therefore has the property that

$$
\lim_{x\to-\infty } x^3 = -\infty.
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $\dfrac{1}{2}$ does not affect the limit at infinity. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{3} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

e-3566.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Constant Function
e-3566.worked_solution:
When we divide the two functions, we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{9{x}^{4}}{3{x}^{4}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }3 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

e-39.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial
e-39.worked_solution:
We identify the leading term and compute its limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{y\to -\infty }(44-3{y}^{4}-9{y}^{12}) & ={lim}_{y\to -\infty }(-9{y}^{12}) \\  & =-{lim}_{y\to -\infty }({y}^{12}) \\  & =-\infty \end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Applying the product rule and the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{f(x)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot ({lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{f(x)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{({lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x))}\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x)=3.$ Therefore, the above becomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{2}$ is an upward parabola, so

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}=\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $\frac{1}{3}$ does not change the sign of the limit. So, we have

$$
